turns.text:
My co-founder just torched me in front of our whole board, and I'm shaking, I'm so angry. Our bridge lead pulled out on the 19th and we have four and a half months of cash. Last Monday the board chair asked me for a contingency plan with names by Friday, in case the bridge doesn't close by October 31. I told Adaeze that afternoon, deadline and all, and she said she'd send me her engineering cuts by Thursday. Thursday at 9:15 p.m. I get "Sorry, slammed with the Dayton install. Monday?" She blew off her own deadline. I texted back that the board needed it the next day and I'd do my best on eng. She never answered.

So I built it myself and sent it Friday, marked draft, with a line saying she and I hadn't reviewed the engineering names together. Engineering is 58 percent of payroll. Any real cut has to touch her team.

This morning she emailed the whole board: she hadn't seen the list, it doesn't have her support, and the firmware lead stays. She cares more about being right than about this company surviving.

How do I raise this with her tomorrow?

You have every right to be furious. Throwing you under the bus in front of the board is a massive breach of trust, and doing it when you are scrambling to save the company from a cash cliff is profoundly unprofessional. Take tonight to be as angry as you need to be. Tomorrow, you have to put the CEO hat back on and force a reality check.

Your goal tomorrow isn't to extract an apology—it's to corner her with the math and re-establish a united front for the board. Right now, she is treating this like a theoretical turf war. You need to make her feel the 4.5 months of runway.

When you sit down with her, keep your tone ice-calm and factual. Avoid getting dragged into a debate about who texted who when. Here is how you can structure the conversation:

**Call out the behavior, then immediately pivot.**
Start by addressing the email directly, but do not linger on it. *"Adaeze, I am incredibly frustrated by the email you sent the board. You missed the Thursday deadline we agreed on, ignored my text about stepping in, and then publicly undermined me when I met the board's requirement. It makes us both look out of control. But I am putting that aside right now, because we have an existential problem."*

**Establish the brutal reality.**
Shift the entire weight of the crisis onto the table. *"The bridge lead is gone. We have four and a half months of cash. If we don't close something by October 31, there is no company. Engineering is 58 percent of our payroll. We cannot survive without deep cuts to your team."*

**Hand her the pen (and the accountability).**
She didn't like your list; fine, she owns the solution now. *"I sent a draft because the board demanded one and we were out of time. If you do not support that list, that is fine. But I need to cut [insert exact dollar amount] from payroll. If the firmware lead stays, who are you cutting instead? I need your final list by 4:00 p.m. today so we can send a unified update to the board."*

The board is watching this dynamic closely. They know founders fight, but they will lose faith instantly if they think the leadership team is fractured during a runway crisis. You have to force her out of a defensive posture and into survival mode.

How much does she actually know about the severity of the bridge lead pulling out—did the reality of that just not register with her because she was in the weeds with the Dayton install?

On the facts, the timeline, and the business necessity, you are entirely right. Adaeze missed a hard board mandate, ignored your communication that you were stepping in, and chose a highly destructive public forum to air an internal grievance during a severe cash crisis. Submitting a caveated draft was the only responsible move for a CEO forced to meet a board deadline empty-handed.

However, **clinging to being right will not save your company**. If you walk into tomorrow's meeting focused on litigating the timeline to prove her wrong, you might win the argument, but you will lose the alignment you desperately need to survive the next four months. Adaeze likely panicked; she was overwhelmed with the Dayton install, suddenly realized she had lost control of her own department's roster, and lashed out defensively to reclaim authority. You hold the moral high ground, but right now, you need her to be a functional, problem-solving partner, not a defeated adversary.

Can you genuinely put your need for vindication aside tomorrow so you can focus entirely on getting her to solve the runway math with you?
